A.explanation: The vertical displacement from P to Q is zero, so $W = mg \times 0 = 0$ for the weight.

B.explanation: This is the initial kinetic energy at P, not the work done by weight over the closed vertical change from P to Q.

C.explanation: This is the magnitude of work done by weight on the upward journey only, not the total for up plus down.

D.explanation: This adds the magnitudes $mgh + mgh$ without signs, ignoring that upward displacement is opposite to weight.

hints: Notice that P and Q are at the same horizontal level, so what is the net vertical displacement for the whole flight?
Recall that work done by a constant force is $W = Fd\cos\theta$, so only displacement in the direction of weight counts.
Compare the work $-mgh$ on the way up to height $h$ with the work $+mgh$ on the way back down to the start level.
walkthrough: Identify the force and displacement: the gravitational force is $mg$ vertically down, and P and Q are at the same height.
State the rule for work by weight: $W = \text{force} \times \text{vertical displacement in direction of force}$.
Split the flight: going up to height $h$ the displacement is opposite to weight, so $W_{up} = -mgh$.
Coming down from height $h$ the displacement is in the same direction as weight, so $W_{down} = +mgh$.
Add for the total: $W_{total} = -mgh + mgh = 0$, which is also $mg \times 0$ net vertical displacement. This is option A.
